examples.title: Projectile in vacuum
examples.description: 20 m/s at 45° on level ground: the range is v² sin 2θ / g = 40.79 m and the flight lasts 2.88 s. The dashed parabola is the closed form; the simulation sits on it.

examples.title: Projectile with quadratic air drag
examples.description: A baseball-like ball (c = 0.006 /m) thrown at 40 m/s and 35°. Compare with the vacuum parabola: the drag shortens the range a lot and makes the descent steeper than the climb.

examples.title: Maximum-range angle with drag
examples.description: With quadratic drag (c = 0.01 /m) the best angle for 40 m/s is 39.5°, below the vacuum 45°. The readout searches for it numerically.

examples.file: 04 Fan of angles from a cliff.kmotion
examples.title: Fan of angles from a cliff
examples.description: Five launch angles from a 30 m cliff at 20 m/s. From a height the farthest shot is flatter than 45°: atan(v / √(v² + 2 g h)).

examples.title: Jump on Earth
examples.description: A 3.5 m/s take-off at 60° from a standing height of 1 m: the jump lasts 0.86 s and covers 1.50 m.

examples.title: Jump on the Moon
examples.description: The same take-off with the Moon's gravity (1.62 m/s²): 4.05 s in the air and 7.08 m, about 4.7 times as far.

examples.title: Simple pendulum: exact against small-angle
examples.description: L = 1 m released at 80°. The small-angle cosine (pink) drifts out of step; the exact elliptic-function solution (green) stays on the simulation. The period is 2.2823 s instead of 2π√(L/g) = 2.0061 s.

examples.title: Damped pendulum
examples.description: Friction at the pivot: the swing decays as e^(−c t/2) and the phase portrait spirals into the origin.

examples.title: Driven damped pendulum: resonance
examples.description: A pendulum with natural frequency 3.13 rad/s driven at 3.0 rad/s: the amplitude builds up to the steady value A / (c ω₀) and then settles. Run the resonance sweep in the Plots tab.

examples.title: Double pendulum: chaos
examples.description: Two pendulums started 0.01° apart. For a few seconds they move together, then they separate exponentially (Lyapunov exponent in the readout) while the energy stays constant.

examples.file: 11 Physical pendulum - a rod on a nail.kmotion
examples.title: Physical pendulum: a rod on a nail
examples.description: A uniform rod swinging about its end behaves like a simple pendulum of length 2L/3. Move the pivot toward the centre to see the period pass through a minimum at L/√12 from the centre.

examples.title: Damped oscillator: underdamped
examples.description: ζ = 0.11: the mass rings down inside the envelope ±A e^(−c t/2m). The closed form lies on the simulation.

examples.title: Damped oscillator: critical damping
examples.description: c = 2√(km): the fastest return to rest without overshooting.

examples.title: Damped oscillator: overdamped
examples.description: ζ > 1: no oscillation, a slow creep back to equilibrium.

examples.title: Driven oscillator at resonance
examples.description: Driven at its natural frequency √(k/m) = 4.47 rad/s. The amplitude F₀ / (c ω₀) is reached after about 2m/c seconds; the phase lag is 90°.

examples.file: 16 Coupled pendulums - normal modes and beats.kmotion
examples.title: Coupled pendulums: normal modes and beats
examples.description: Two pendulums joined by a spring. Pull one and the energy swaps back and forth (beats); start in mode 1 or mode 2 and it stays a pure sine at ω = √(g/L) or √(g/L + 2k/m).

examples.title: Five coupled oscillators
examples.description: Five masses in a chain: five normal modes with different frequencies. Mode 2 is shown; the plot of modal amplitudes shows only that mode is excited.

examples.title: Atwood machine
examples.description: Masses 3 kg and 2 kg over an ideal pulley: a = (m₁ − m₂) g / (m₁ + m₂) = 1.96 m/s², tension 23.5 N. Add a pulley mass and a drops.

examples.file: 19 Block on an incline with friction.kmotion
examples.title: Block on an incline with friction
examples.description: θ = 35°, μs = 0.5, μk = 0.3: tan 35° = 0.70 > μs so the block slides with a = g (sin θ − μk cos θ) = 3.2 m/s². Lower the angle below 26.6° (arctan 0.5) and it stays put.

examples.title: Rolling race down an incline
examples.description: A block, a ring, a cylinder and two spheres released together. Rolling objects are slower than the sliding block by 1 + I/mr²; the solid sphere wins and the ring comes last, whatever their masses and radii.

examples.title: Elastic collision in 1-D
examples.description: A 2 kg cart at 3 m/s hits a 1 kg cart at −1 m/s with e = 1. Momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved: the velocities after are 0.33 and 4.33 m/s.

examples.title: Perfectly inelastic collision
examples.description: Same carts with e = 0: they move together at the centre-of-mass velocity and kinetic energy is lost: ½ μ (1 − e²) v_rel².

examples.title: Billiard collision at right angles
examples.description: A cue ball hits an equal ball at rest off-centre. With equal masses and e = 1 the two balls leave at exactly 90° to each other.

examples.title: Breaking a billiard rack
examples.description: The cue ball hits fifteen balls in a triangle. Event-driven physics: each collision is resolved at its exact time. Momentum is conserved until the cushions are hit.

examples.title: Newton's cradle (planck)
examples.description: Five steel balls on strings, rigid-body physics with planck: one ball in, one ball out. Lift two or three balls with the parameter panel.

examples.title: Ballistic pendulum
examples.description: A 10 g bullet at 300 m/s embeds in a 1 kg block on a 1.5 m string. Momentum gives V = m v / (m + M) = 2.97 m/s; energy gives the rise h = V²/2g = 0.45 m and the swing angle 45.6°. Only 1% of the kinetic energy survives the impact.

examples.title: Circular orbit
examples.description: A planet at 1 AU around a one solar-mass star: period 1 yr and speed 2π AU/yr (29.8 km/s). Kepler III: T²/a³ = 1.

examples.title: Elliptical orbit: Kepler's laws
examples.description: e = 0.6, perihelion 1 AU (a = 2.5 AU): the wedges swept in equal times have equal areas (II), r + r′ = 2a for the empty focus (I) and T²/a³ = 1 (III), all checked live.

examples.title: Binary star
examples.description: Two equal masses orbiting their common centre of mass.

examples.title: Escape speed
examples.description: Fire a probe straight up from 1 AU at 90% of the escape speed: it climbs to 5.3 AU and falls back. At 100% it just escapes (a parabola). The escape speed is √2 times the circular speed.

examples.title: Hohmann transfer: Earth to Mars
examples.description: Two burns: Δv₁ = 2.95 km/s at departure, Δv₂ = 2.65 km/s at arrival, 259 days of flight. Mars must lead Earth by 44.4° at launch.

examples.title: Gravity assist at Jupiter
examples.description: A probe passes behind Jupiter: in the planet frame its speed is unchanged but its direction turns, and in the Sun frame it leaves much faster, with the energy taken from Jupiter's orbital motion.

examples.title: Restricted three-body: the Arenstorf orbit
examples.description: A light spacecraft in the rotating Earth-Moon frame follows a periodic orbit (period 17.065) that visits the Moon twice per lap. The Jacobi constant stays fixed.

examples.title: Tadpole orbit around L4
examples.description: A body just inside the Lagrange point L4 of the Earth-Moon system circles it in a small, stable tadpole orbit (L4 is stable for μ < 0.0385). The Jacobi constant stays fixed.

examples.title: Trojan asteroids of Jupiter
examples.description: The Sun-Jupiter problem (μ = 0.000954): an asteroid on a slightly wider orbit than L4 librates along a long tadpole that reaches towards Jupiter, as the Trojans do. Switch on the inertial frame to see the bodies circle.

examples.title: Figure-eight three-body
examples.description: Three equal masses follow the same eight-shaped curve, one third of a period apart (Chenciner–Montgomery, 2000). The period is 6.32591398 in units where G = m = 1.

examples.title: Inner solar system
examples.description: Sun, Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars from real orbital elements (J2000), integrated as an N-body problem with velocity-Verlet. The periods come out as 87.97, 224.7, 365.2 and 687 days.

examples.title: Disc galaxy
examples.description: 120 light bodies on circular orbits around a heavy centre, with softened gravity. Switch on Barnes–Hut and the 3-D view.

examples.file: 39 Ramp and a pile of boxes.kmotion
examples.title: Ramp and a pile of boxes
examples.description: Ramp and a pile of boxes: a rigid-body world (planck). Press Play, drag a body with the mouse to throw it, or edit it in the Sandbox tools.

examples.file: 40 Car with a motor and suspension.kmotion
examples.title: Car with a motor and suspension
examples.description: Car with a motor and suspension: a rigid-body world (planck). Press Play, drag a body with the mouse to throw it, or edit it in the Sandbox tools.

examples.title: Pulley (Atwood machine)
examples.description: Pulley (Atwood machine): a rigid-body world (planck). Press Play, drag a body with the mouse to throw it, or edit it in the Sandbox tools.

examples.title: Chain of hinged links
examples.description: Chain of hinged links: a rigid-body world (planck). Press Play, drag a body with the mouse to throw it, or edit it in the Sandbox tools.

examples.title: Seesaw and a dropped ball
examples.description: Seesaw and a dropped ball: a rigid-body world (planck). Press Play, drag a body with the mouse to throw it, or edit it in the Sandbox tools.

examples.file: 44 Motorised slider and a welded T.kmotion
examples.title: Motorised slider and a welded T
examples.description: Motorised slider and a welded T: a rigid-body world (planck). Press Play, drag a body with the mouse to throw it, or edit it in the Sandbox tools.

examples.title: Centripetal force
examples.description: A 1 kg mass on a 2 m string at 6 m/s: a = v²/R = 18 m/s² towards the centre, tension 18 N. Tick “Cut the string” and it leaves along the tangent.

examples.title: Banked curve
examples.description: A 60 m curve banked at 15°: the ideal speed is √(R g tan θ) = 12.6 m/s; with μ = 0.3 the car may go as fast as 19.1 m/s before it skids out.

examples.title: Conical pendulum
examples.description: L = 1.2 m at 35°: the bob circles with period 2π√(L cos θ / g) = 1.99 s. Change the speed ratio and the cone breathes.

examples.title: Coriolis force on a turntable
examples.description: A ball rolls from the centre of a disc turning at 0.8 rad/s. On the ground it moves in a straight line; on the disc it curves. Switch the view to see both.

examples.title: Spinning top
examples.description: A fast top (150 rad/s) precesses slowly at m g d / (I₃ ω₃) = 3.9 rad/s while it nutates at about I₃ω₃/I₁ = 100 rad/s.
